# Three Years in, CVRT’s Targeted Approach Has Been on Target


November 17, 2026


*Q&A with[Jon Vacko](https://www.calamos.com/about/portfolio-management/jon-vacko/) , CFA, and[Joe Wysocki](https://www.calamos.com/about/portfolio-management/joseph-wysocki/) , CFA*


For investors who want exposure to growth companies with a potentially less exposure to downside,[Calamos Convertible Equity Alternative ETF (CVRT)](https://www.calamos.com/funds/etf/calamos-convertible-equity-alternative-cvrt/) has delivered compelling results since its inception three years ago. The fund’s targeted approach to equity-sensitive convertibles has delivered an average annualized NAV return of 22.68% over the life of the fund through October 31, 2026, strongly outperforming the convertible market’s gain of 14.94%.* We sat down with Senior Co-Portfolio Managers Jon Vacko and Joe Wysocki to find out more.


## Q. What’s CVRT designed to do and why do you think the fund has been so successful over the past three years?


**Jon Vacko (JV):** We believe CVRT provides a way for investors to participate in some of the most exciting growth companies in the market today, with potentially less risk than investing in their equities outright. Convertibles have a lot of moving parts and can be used in different ways, but Calamos has been investing in convertible securities since the 1970s. I think this experience gave us a real advantage in designing CVRT to provide targeted exposure to a particular area of the convertible market.


## Q. How do convertible securities change the risk/reward equation for equity investors?


**Joe Wysocki (JW):** Convertible securities blend characteristics of stocks and bonds. There are different types of convertible securities, but we can keep things simple and focus on convertible bonds—which have maturity dates, are issued at par, and provide coupon income. What changes the risk/reward equation is that the convertible can be converted into shares of the issuer’s equity at a predetermined price. This conversion feature means that the convertible tends to rise alongside its underlying equity, while the bond characteristics can provide some ballast if the stock declines.


The level of upside participation and downside risk mitigation for any convertible changes over time and varies from one convertible to the next. Some convertibles offer the potential to cushion more equity downside, and some are more equity sensitive with more exposure to the upside and downside of their underlying equities. CVRT falls into this second category—our universe is the more equity-sensitive part of the convertible market, but with some more ballast versus investing in the company’s stock.


## Q. What makes the convertible market exciting today?


**JV:** The convertible market is exciting because of the companies in it. Convertibles have been a popular choice for companies seeking access to capital to fund growth. Since the very first convertibles were issued by US railroad companies more than 200 years ago, the convertible market has been home to the companies at the forefront of progress. Like the age of the railroads, today’s convertible market is full of companies driving secular change across the economy, not just technology and AI, but also health care and defense.


The convertible market has tended to tilt toward smaller and mid-cap companies, but we’re seeing more and more mega-cap companies issue convertibles as well. This year, that’s included companies like Alphabet, Meta and Oracle, all of which issued a type of convertible that’s particularly equity sensitive—a mandatory convertible, which, as the name implies, converts to equity on a set date. So, we’re seeing a lot of convertibles come to market that fit into CVRT’s universe.


And these companies are part of a bigger story about issuance: The market set records for new issuance in 2025, and those have already been broken in 2026 with more than $225 billion coming to market through October. We wouldn’t be surprised if issuance slows down over the near term as potential issuers evaluate fiscal and monetary policy uncertainties, but our expectation is that healthy issuance levels can continue.


## Q. What’s your outlook for the convertible market, and for CVRT?


**JW:** The markets are in a period of rotation. Typically, elections bring clarity, but this time, there’s more uncertainty than usual as investors wait to see how the “blue wave” plays out—will we see policy shifts or gridlock?


Even when we factor in these unknowns, our team sees a lot of opportunities, and the convertible structure is ideal for navigating volatile markets. With all the high-growth and AI-related companies in the convertible market, it wasn’t surprising to see some gains given back after midterms. But in the days following the election, we saw convertibles do their job, with many holding up better than their underlying equities.


What’s important to remember is that, at its core, the convertible market has been a market of innovation and growth. Many of today’s leading companies, like Apple and Microsoft, issued convertibles when they were less established, so we can see that the convertible market is home to many of the “leaders of tomorrow.”


Today’s convertible issuers are also at the forefront of powerful secular growth trends, which can provide a powerful “wind in the sails” over the long-term, even though the pace of change may vary and market leadership may shift over shorter periods. Growth companies find ways to adapt to changing conditions, and I believe that will continue to be the case. Technological progress, health care breakthroughs and a quest for productivity aren’t going to stop. Convertible issuers will be an important part of the story, and this sets up well for CVRT.
